title: Broadcom Rides Rocketing Trend For Custom AI Accelerators
gist: Broadcom's Hock Tan guided AI-related chip revenue from $2.6 billion in fiscal 2022 to $230 billion by fiscal 2028 — two orders of magnitude — on the back of six custom XPU customers representing roughly 30 gigawatts of compute, with Anthropic overtaking Google as the largest XPU buyer in 2027 and OpenAI's 'Jalapeno' ASIC pushing Google to number three by 2028. The piece argues custom XPUs cost roughly $12-15 billion per gigawatt versus $18-40 billion for Nvidia rackscale systems, and that 'chip shepherding' is a structurally better business than selling finished silicon.

themes.theme: The $230 billion forecast and bubble pushback

insights.claim: Broadcom's custom AI XPU business plus AI networking and related AI system chippery is forecast to grow from $2.6 billion in fiscal 2022 to $230 billion in fiscal 2028 — two orders of magnitude in six years.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A single supplier guiding to $230B of AI revenue is the most aggressive concrete number on the table for the custom-silicon leg of the AI trade.
insights.locator: Broadcom was already helping Google get its homegrown TPUs

insights.claim: The $230 billion figure is put in perspective as comparable to worldwide pizza consumption in 2024 and roughly a quarter of the $1 trillion US military budget for the fiscal year just ended.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: The scale comparison is the implicit skeptic's flag: a single product line approaching national-budget magnitude invites mean-reversion risk.
insights.locator: The US military budget for the fiscal year

insights.claim: Broadcom has already secured the HBM memory, chip wafers, and packaging needed to fulfil the forecast revenue stream, and Hock Tan said it can add more capacity if demand runs higher.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Pre-secured HBM and packaging means the forecast is supply-backed, not aspirational — and it locks capacity away from rivals.
insights.locator: Broadcom has secured the HBM memory, chip wafers, and packaging

insights.claim: Hock Tan deliberately warned Wall Street not to expect quarterly updates to the multi-year forecast, using the disclosure instead to tell investors to stop worrying about a GenAI bubble bursting.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A management team issuing a long-dated, non-updatable forecast is making a deliberate sentiment intervention — treat subsequent silence as designed, not as deterioration.
insights.quote: basically to tell Wall Street to take a chill pill on the GenAI bubble bursting
insights.locator: Tan warned Wall Street to not expect quarterly updates

themes.theme: Customer concentration and the gigawatt league table

insights.claim: Broadcom has six custom XPU customers — Google, Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta Platforms confirmed, with ByteDance or Apple speculated for the other two — collectively representing about 30 gigawatts of total compute capacity.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: 30 GW across six accounts quantifies just how concentrated — and therefore fragile — the custom-silicon revenue base is.
insights.locator: Across the six XPU customers that Broadcom has

insights.claim: Anthropic is deploying 1 gigawatt of Ironwood TPU 7 accelerators this year, 5 gigawatts of TPU 8i systems in 2027, and wants 10 gigawatts of the follow-on TPU 9 in 2028, making it Broadcom's largest XPU customer in 2027 and 2028.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A 10x capacity ramp in two years at a single private model builder is the clearest signal of how fast frontier-lab compute budgets are compounding.
insights.locator: Anthropic is deploying 1 gigawatt of

insights.claim: Anthropic buying more TPU hardware than Google itself is explained by Google being a cloud whose customers demand Nvidia GPUs, so Google's own TPU consumption is constrained by what its external customers want.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Cloud providers cannot fully self-supply silicon because end-customer preference for CUDA forces continued Nvidia purchases — a durable floor under Nvidia demand.
insights.quote: But Google is a cloud, and cloud customers want Nvidia GPUs.
insights.locator: As one of the AI model builders with tons of cash flow

insights.claim: OpenAI has picked Broadcom to shepherd its 'Jalapeno' XPU, is on track to buy 1.3 gigawatts of Jalapeno cluster hardware in 2027 and another 5 gigawatts of Jalapeno and its follow-on in 2028, making it Broadcom's second-biggest XPU customer and pushing Google to number three.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: The model builders, not the clouds, become the dominant buyers of custom silicon — a reordering of who holds pricing power in the supply chain.
insights.locator: OpenAI has chosen Broadcom to do its chip shepherding

insights.claim: The follow-on OpenAI chip is approaching tapeout and Broadcom and OpenAI are already working on a third-generation XPU design, indicating a locked-in multi-generation engagement.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Design-win stickiness across three generations makes this revenue far harder for Marvell or others to dislodge.
insights.locator: The follow-on OpenAI chip, which we do not know the code-name of

insights.claim: Broadcom will deliver three generations of Meta MTIA devices between now and the end of fiscal 2027, with visibility on 3 gigawatts of capacity through the end of fiscal 2028.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Meta's 3 GW is an order of magnitude smaller than Anthropic's 2028 ask — useful for sizing relative AI ambition across hyperscalers.
insights.locator: With Meta Platforms, Broadcom will deliver three generations

insights.claim: Amazon Web Services is not a full XPU design customer but is using Broadcom for packaging and integration on Trainium 4, showing Broadcom monetizes even accounts it does not fully own.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Packaging-only engagements widen Broadcom's reach beyond the headline six customers.
insights.locator: but Amazon Web Services is using Broadcom for packaging

insights.claim: Custom XPU systems can be installed for roughly $12 billion per gigawatt excluding CPUs, memory and racks, or about $15 billion per gigawatt fully loaded — against $18 billion per gigawatt for Nvidia Grace-Hopper systems and $40 billion per gigawatt for Nvidia Vera-Rubin systems.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Dollars per gigawatt is emerging as the unit of comparison for AI infrastructure, and custom silicon undercuts Nvidia's newest rack by more than half.
insights.locator: there is about 30 gigawatts of total compute capacity

insights.claim: Hock Tan claims Broadcom has consistently delivered the fastest time to market for TPUs from product definition to production without resubmits, and calls this a very deep moat for competitors to cross.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: First-pass silicon success, not IP, is the stated moat — a process advantage rivals cannot buy quickly.
insights.quote: We have consistently delivered the fastest time to market for TPUs from product definition to production without the need for resubmits. We believe these are very deep moats for any competitor to cross.
insights.locator: Tan said on the call with Wall Street

insights.claim: Talk of Marvell, MediaTek or Alchip stealing Google's TPU business is dismissed because the real gating factor is who gets HBM memory allocations rather than design capability.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: If HBM allocation is the true moat, track memory supply agreements rather than design-win headlines when handicapping ASIC competition.
insights.quote: It is all about who gets the HBM allocations anyway.
insights.locator: So forget all of the talk about Marvell

insights.claim: Being a 'chip shepherd' that indulges the egos of tech titans is argued to be a structurally better business than selling a finished XPU or CPU to them, because none of the titans want to use what their rivals use except x86 CPUs and Nvidia or AMD GPUs — and they only tolerate those because of cloud customer demand and capacity shortages.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Explains why the merchant-silicon model is squeezed while the design-services model expands — a lens for valuing Broadcom versus Intel or AMD.
insights.quote: It is so much better to be a chip shepherd indulging the egos of the tech titans then to try to sell a finished XPU or CPU to them.
insights.locator: Say what you will, but Tan knows how to squeeze

insights.claim: Broadcom's AI boom is dominated by networking rather than XPUs, with the 100 Gb/sec and 200 Gb/sec SerDes variants of the Tomahawk 6 Ethernet switch ASIC selling strongly and every hyperscaler using Broadcom for XPU shepherding also using Tomahawk 6 for scale-out.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: The XPU design win is a wedge that pulls in higher-volume networking attach — the real compounding revenue engine.
insights.locator: The AI boom inside of Broadcom is not just AI XPUs

insights.claim: The Tomahawk Ultra variant, which cuts Ethernet stack latency enough to be used for scale-up coherent memory interconnect inside rackscale machines, is seeing surprising adoption and is already deploying at some customers with the ramp running through fiscal 2027.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Ethernet encroaching on scale-up coherent interconnect is the first real threat to NVLink's most defensible territory.
insights.locator: The Tomahawk Ultra variant of the 6 series chips

insights.claim: The unannounced 204.8 Tb/sec Tomahawk 7 Ethernet switch ASIC, using 400 Gb/sec SerDes to give 3.2 Tb/sec per port across eight lanes, has already taped out and should appear in switches in early calendar 2028 or possibly late calendar 2027.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A concrete 2027-2028 bandwidth doubling to price into optics, cabling and switch-vendor forecasts.
insights.locator: And by the way, the 204.8 Tb/sec Tomahawk 7

insights.claim: With the CPU total addressable market projected to grow from $26 billion in 2025 to $220 billion by 2030 and every hyperscaler building its own Arm server CPU, Broadcom is expected to branch into CPU shepherding — focused on packaging with some design work, as it already does with Fujitsu's forthcoming Monaka Arm server CPU.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: An unpriced second leg of growth: a nearly 10x CPU TAM expansion that Broadcom can attack with the same asset-light model.
insights.locator: I fully expect for Broadcom to start shepherding CPUs

insights.claim: Broadcom will not design and sell its own Arm server chip to the tech titans, a stance traced back to it selling off the Vulcan processor to Cavium Networks years ago.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Confirms Broadcom stays out of head-to-head merchant CPU competition — it monetizes the trend without taking product risk.
insights.locator: I do not think Broadcom has any interest in designing

insights.claim: An external CPU may remain the safest architecture because a large, albeit slower, CPU memory address space benefits XPUs that must skimp on HBM or other stacked memories due to capacity scarcity.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Memory scarcity shapes system architecture, arguing against fully integrated CPU-on-XPU designs and for continued discrete CPU demand.
insights.locator: But I also think that having a big memory address space

insights.claim: Fujitsu and all six XPU customers use Broadcom's 3.5D Extreme Dimension System in Package chiplet stacking, which puts stacked DRAM and stacked CPU chiplets into a single package.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A proprietary packaging standard adopted by every major customer is a lock-in mechanism separate from the design work itself.
insights.locator: Fujitsu as well as the six XPU customers are using

insights.claim: In the third quarter ended in early August, Broadcom booked $29.59 billion in sales, up 85.5 percent year on year and 33.4 percent sequentially, with operating income of $15.96 billion (up 2.71X) and net income up 3.17X to $13.09 billion, or 44.2 percent of revenues.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: 44 percent net margin on 85 percent revenue growth is the operating leverage case for the AI infrastructure complex.
insights.locator: In the third quarter ended in early August

insights.claim: AI-related revenues reached $16.74 billion in the quarter, up 3.22X year on year and 54 percent sequentially, split as $12.22 billion for AI compute and $4.52 billion for AI networking.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Roughly 57 percent of total company revenue is now AI, and a 54 percent sequential jump sets a very high bar for future comparisons.
insights.locator: AI-related revenues added up to $16.74 billion

insights.claim: Broadcom's Infrastructure Software group, which includes VMware, generated $8.75 billion of sales at an 84 percent operating margin described as IBM mainframe-class, with an estimated $5.52 billion of that coming from VMware licenses and support.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: The software leg quietly funds the AI leg at mainframe-like margins — a cushion that pure-play AI names lack.
insights.locator: The Infrastructure Software group, which includes VMware

insights.claim: Broadcom ended the quarter with $23.98 billion in cash but still carries $59.42 billion of debt from the VMware acquisition.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: The leverage from VMware remains the balance-sheet vulnerability if AI order growth stalls.
insights.locator: Broadcom ended the quarter with $23.98 billion in cash
